summary:
Every room number is between 1 and n, so it also names a slot of the array (`room − 1`). That lets the
array itself record which rooms have been seen, either with a sign or by adding n per booking, so no
extra memory is needed. Adding n even keeps the answer in increasing order for free.

question.md:
`bookings` has n entries, each a room number from 1 to n, and no room appears more than twice. Return
the rooms that appear **exactly twice**, in increasing order.

- **Values 1 … n and length n:** every value is a valid index after subtracting 1. That's the
  property every clever approach here relies on.
- **At most twice** means "seen before" is enough to identify a double booking: there's never a third
  copy to worry about.
- **Sorted output**, even though the bookings come in any order.
- **The challenge:** O(n) time with O(1) extra space besides the answer. A count array would be O(n)
  extra space.

think.md:
Take `bookings = [5, 1, 4, 5, 2, 1, 7]` (n = 7). Rooms 1 and 5 each appear twice: the answer is
`[1, 5]`.

The easy way is a count array with one slot per room. But look at the input: it **is** an array with
one slot per room. Slot 0 can stand for room 1, slot 1 for room 2, and so on. We just need to record
information in it **without destroying** the values still to be read.

panels.label: slot i stands for room i + 1

think.caption: Each slot keeps its own value and can also carry a mark for its room.

think.md:
Two ways to keep both pieces of information in one slot:

- **Sign:** values are positive, so making a slot negative can mean "this room was seen", and
  `abs()` still recovers the value.
- **Adding n:** values are at most n, so adding n once per booking stores a count in the "tens place";
  `(x − 1) mod n + 1` recovers the original value and `(x − 1) div n` the count.

approaches.title: Count each room by scanning

idea.md: For each room 1 … n, count its bookings with a full scan; rooms with count 2 go into the answer, which comes out sorted because rooms are checked in order.

build: For each room `x` from 1 to n, count how many bookings equal `x`.

lines.text: Rooms in increasing order, each counted with a full scan. Count 2 means double-booked.

notes.c: Append into `out` and grow `*returnSize`; at most n/2 rooms can be doubled, so n slots is plenty.

lines.text: Already sorted, because rooms were checked from 1 upwards.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²):** n scans of n bookings. **Space O(1)** besides the answer.

walk.title: For each room 1 … n, scan the bookings and count it.

limits.md: Every room needs its own full scan. One pass that tallies all rooms at once replaces n passes.

approaches.title: Count array

idea.md: One pass fills `count[room]`. A second pass over rooms 1 … n collects those with count 2, in increasing order.

build: Collect every room `x` with `count[x] == 2`, from 1 to n.

lines.text: Rooms are 1 … n, so they index the count array directly (slot 0 unused).
Walking rooms upward gives the answer already sorted.

notes.c: Free the counts; the caller frees `out`.

steps.text: Rooms with count 2, left to right: [1, 5].

walk.title: Tally bookings per room in a count array, then read the rooms with count 2 in order.

limits.md: The count array duplicates something we already have: an array of n slots indexed by room. The problem asks for O(1) extra space, so the marks should go into the input itself.

approaches.title: Mark seen rooms with a minus sign

idea.md:
Read each value `v` as `abs(v)` (it may have been negated already). Look at slot `v − 1`: if it's
negative, room `v` was seen before, so it's double-booked; otherwise negate it to mark room `v` as
seen. Duplicates are discovered in input order, so sort them at the end, and flip the signs back so
the caller's array is unchanged.

build: For each index i: `v = abs(bookings[i])`, `j = v − 1`.
Restore every slot with `abs`, sort the answer, return it.

lines.text: The value here may already carry a mark (a minus sign put there by an earlier booking), so `abs` recovers the room number. Its flag lives in slot `room − 1`.
The flag is already set: this is the room's second booking (there's never a third).
First time: set the flag by negating the slot. The slot's own value survives as its absolute value.
Undo the marks so the caller gets their array back unchanged.
Duplicates were found in input order, so sort them.

complexity.md: **Time O(n + d log d)** for d double-booked rooms (at most n/2): one pass plus sorting the answer. **Space O(1)** extra besides the answer.

steps.text: Every value is a room 1 … n, so `value − 1` is a valid slot. A negative slot means 'that room was seen'.
Read 5 (index 0): slot 4 was positive. Flip it to mark room 5 as seen.
Read 1 (index 1): slot 0 was positive. Flip it to mark room 1 as seen.
Read 4 (index 2): slot 3 was positive. Flip it to mark room 4 as seen.
Read 5 (index 3): slot 4 is already negative, so room 5 was seen before. Twice!
Read 2 (index 4): slot 1 was positive. Flip it to mark room 2 as seen.
Read 1 (index 5): slot 0 is already negative, so room 1 was seen before. Twice!
Read 7 (index 6): slot 6 was positive. Flip it to mark room 7 as seen.
Found in reading order [5, 1]; sort to get [1, 5].

walk.title: Use the sign of slot v − 1 as a 'room v seen' flag. Meeting an already negative slot means a second booking.

limits.md: The sign only says "seen or not", so duplicates are noticed in input order and must be sorted. Storing a small **count** in each slot instead lets a final left-to-right pass emit them already sorted.

approaches.title: Count in place by adding n

idea.md:
For every booking of room `v`, add n to slot `v − 1`. A slot's original value is between 1 and n,
so after the pass slot `i` holds `original + n × (bookings of room i + 1)`:

- the original value is `(x − 1) mod n + 1` (that's how each value is read during the pass,
  even if n has already been added to it);
- the room was booked twice exactly when `x > 2n`.

A final pass over slots 0 … n − 1 lists double-booked rooms in increasing order and restores
every slot.

build: For each index i: `v = (bookings[i] − 1) mod n + 1`, then `bookings[v − 1] += n`.
For each slot i in order: if `bookings[i] > 2n`, append room `i + 1`.

lines.text: Recover the room stored at `i`, then add n to that room's slot: one "tick" per booking. A slot can reach n + 2n = 3n ≤ 3 × 10⁵, far from overflowing. `(x − 1) mod n + 1` peels the ticks off: the original value minus 1 is in 0 … n − 1, so the remainder is untouched by multiples of n.
Two ticks push a slot above 2n (its original value is at least 1). Reading slots left to right lists the rooms in increasing order, with no sorting.
Remove the ticks so the caller's array is exactly as it was.

complexity.md: **Time O(n):** two passes. **Space O(1)** extra besides the answer, and the input ends up unchanged.

steps.text: n = 7. Read each value as (value − 1) mod n + 1 so additions made earlier don't hide it.
Slots above 2n = 14 were bumped twice: rooms [1, 5], already in order. Then each slot is restored with (value − 1) mod n + 1.

walk.title: Add n to slot v − 1 for every booking of room v. Afterwards slot i holds original + n × (bookings of room i + 1).

takeaways.md:
- When values are `1 … n` in an array of length n, **value − 1 is an index**, so the array can be its
  own lookup table.
- Hide extra information in a slot without losing its value: flip the **sign** for a yes/no flag, or
  add **multiples of n** for a small count (read back with `mod` and `div`).
- Undo the marks afterwards if the caller might still use the array.
